j.learned_fact: An empty tummy makes a growling sound, which means you are hungry; the dog's does too.
j.thinking_skill: Inferring a cause (hunger) from a bodily sensation and checking it by eating
j.notes: The dog Ben appears out of nowhere at the end, and the hot bench and knife are safety beats bolted on with no plot role. Choppy, unparagraphed text.

j.learned_fact: The tiny lines on fingertips are fingerprints, and no two people, not even twins, have the same ones.
j.thinking_skill: Using physical evidence to rule himself out and identify a culprit
j.notes: The fingerprint clue is never actually used to identify Kit (her frosting-covered fingers do that), so the fact is decorative. 'Lunchtime' at a hockey game and the shining ice are filler; sentences run a touch long for a 5-year-old.

j.learned_fact: A seed sends its root down first and its shoot up toward the light, even if the seed was planted upside down.
j.thinking_skill: Making a prediction (plant will grow into the floor), observing, and revising it
j.notes: The monkey drawing and the S-E-E-D spelling are bolted-on early-literacy beats unrelated to the plot. Short and effective otherwise.

j.learned_fact: Children grow while they sleep, and a steady bedtime routine (bath, book, lights out) helps sleep come fast and last all night.
j.thinking_skill: Measuring change against a fixed landmark (comparing his head to the branch he stood under in fall)
j.notes: Growth is compressed so that a few nights of good sleep read as the cause of a visible height gain; the causal link between the bedtime routine and heading the ball is looser than the story implies. The 'First, Next, Then, Last' sequence is slightly formulaic.

j.learned_fact: A square frame squashes into a diamond but a triangle holds its shape, so triangles make a sturdy roof.
j.thinking_skill: trial-and-error comparison leading to a general rule
j.notes: 'Mattress', 'ill' and 'quiet room' are slightly planted, but the warm framing (cookies for a sick mom) carries the structural lesson naturally.

j.learned_fact: The pupil (the black dot in the middle of the eye) shrinks in bright light and grows larger in the dark.
j.thinking_skill: repeating a test (light on/off) to confirm a cause-and-effect observation
j.notes: The pupil discovery has nothing to do with the batting lesson beyond a pun on 'eyes wide open'; the 'had been ill' sentence and the ribbon prize are bolted on to tick vocabulary.

j.learned_fact: The brain uses about 20 percent of the body's energy while weighing only about 2 percent of it; a product is the answer when two numbers are multiplied (6 x 4 = 24). Misleading inference: the story implies hard thinking noticeably raises energy use, but the brain's share barely changes with mental effort.
j.thinking_skill: Proportional reasoning (a small thing can use a large share) and checking a hunch against a reference source
j.notes: A spelling test with a 'math section' exists only to plant the word 'product'; the hunger explanation is a common misconception dressed as discovery. Voice is otherwise lively and age-true.

j.learned_fact: A pinhole box safely projects an upside-down image of the Sun, so you can watch an eclipse turn into a crescent without looking at the Sun.
j.thinking_skill: Classifying items by two attributes at once (line/space and high/low)
j.notes: Two unrelated lessons share one story; the 'four piles' of notes is a contrived classification that does not actually teach note reading. The immigrant grandfather 'who built things' and the retreat indoors are bolted-on prompt items.

j.learned_fact: The three interior angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees, so a missing angle can be found by subtracting the two known ones (60 + 70 = 130, so 50).
j.thinking_skill: deductive calculation of an unknown angle from a general rule
j.notes: The kite is treated as a triangle for the math but is called 'a small bright square' in the sky at the end; the repair (cut along the line, then tape a scrap into the gap) is muddled, and the right-angle/360 aside is recited rather than needed.

j.learned_fact: Light bends where it leaves the water, so a fish looks shallower than it really is; to catch it you aim below where it appears.
j.thinking_skill: inferring an invisible cause from a repeated failure and testing a corrected strategy
j.notes: Maya is 'on dinner strike' and then takes Declan off her 'boycott list', a loose use of boycott; the citation/corrosive care-sheet opening is a slightly artificial way to seat two vocabulary words.

j.learned_fact: Teenagers' body clocks shift later than young children's, so they naturally get sleepy around 10:30-11 pm, which is why an early first bell suits small children better than teens.
j.thinking_skill: gathering data to test a hypothesis and recognising that a one-person sample is not enough
j.notes: 'She recounted' is a misuse (recount means to narrate past events, not read out a draft); the eventual five data points are still tiny, though the story is honest about needing more.

j.learned_fact: Breathing is driven mainly by the diaphragm, and a hiccup is a sudden spasm of that muscle with the vocal cords snapping shut; slow deep breathing can calm it.
j.thinking_skill: Applying a remembered mechanism (diaphragm spasm) to design a remedy and testing it
j.notes: The deodorant and hiccup episodes are two hygiene prompts stitched together; 'cooperate' is forced. The remedy works instantly, which is convenient.

j.learned_fact: A car's airbag is triggered by a deceleration sensor, inflates in about 30 milliseconds via a chemical charge that produces nitrogen gas, then deflates through vents, so it is already flat before you finish blinking.
j.thinking_skill: changing one variable at a time to isolate a bug
j.notes: The debugging logic is inconsistent: the comparison is described as greater-than at the start, he flips it to less-than, then flips it 'back to greater-than' and the same code now behaves differently. The voice and the uncle scene are excellent.

j.learned_fact: A random sample can represent a much larger group, and the sample size needed does not depend on how big the population is, as long as the draw is random ('stir first').
j.thinking_skill: Designing a random-sampling experiment and reasoning about why randomness matters for representativeness
j.notes: The demonstration re-samples 42 slips she has already counted, so it shows sample-to-population agreement only loosely, and the 'same thousand either way' claim is asserted rather than explained. Register reads slightly young for a 9th grader.

j.learned_fact: Paying only a $25 minimum on a $1,000 credit-card balance takes about five and a half years and costs over $600 in interest, while paying $100 a month clears it in under a year (the figures are consistent with roughly 20% APR).
j.thinking_skill: Modeling a repayment schedule and changing one input (monthly payment) to compare long-run outcomes
j.notes: The interest rate is never stated, so a reader cannot check the arithmetic without assuming one. Priya being 18 with a robotics build costing a thousand dollars sits a little old for a 14-year-old reader, though the prose is accessible.

j.learned_fact: Benford's law (about 30 percent of leading digits are 1, under 5 percent are 9) only detects fabricated numbers when the data vary naturally; fixed prices like a 9-dollar ticket break that assumption, so the test says nothing about honesty.
j.thinking_skill: checking whether a statistical test's assumptions hold before acting on its result
j.notes: A 19-dollar entry is found in the 'mountain of nines' pile though it starts with 1; the four-hundred-dollar discrepancy is left open (deliberately). Vocabulary (impetuous, obfuscate, fortitude) is used correctly.

j.learned_fact: Spreading the same number of study hours over many days produces better retention than concentrating them in a few long sessions (the spacing effect).
j.thinking_skill: Distinguishing a testable explanation from an unfalsifiable one ('she's just smart') and holding hours constant to compare study schedules
j.notes: Alicia's evidence is anecdotal (two cousins, her own French words) and she admits it proves nothing, so the reader gets the idea without any stated research; the rowing parallel is elegant but the pacing analogy is not the same mechanism as spacing. Very strong prose, arguably a shade above a 15-year-old.

j.learned_fact: Doubling an object's length multiplies its surface area and cross-section by 4 but its volume and weight by 8 (square-cube law), which is why giant insects cannot exist and elephants need thick legs.
j.thinking_skill: quantitative proportional reasoning plus recognising the limits of what the model can decide
j.notes: Minor typo ('two in night in February'); the 1.5x figures (about 3.4 and about 2.25) are correct and the 'math is a floor, not a map' reflection is earned rather than tacked on.

j.learned_fact: The first web page went online at CERN in 1991, CERN released the technology royalty-free in 1993, and a restored copy of that first page is still online.
j.thinking_skill: Counterfactual reasoning about ownership of the web, plus catching and checking her own wish to over-generalize
j.notes: Long, and Marcus reading the fact 'off a crumpled printout' is a contrivance. 'Mendacity' and 'enthralled' are slightly ornamental. Otherwise the most complete story in the set.

j.learned_fact: GPS satellite clocks would run about 38 microseconds a day fast without relativistic correction, and errors would grow by kilometers per day; a receiver times signals from at least four satellites.
j.thinking_skill: Reasoning about correctness as a stack of layers, each of which must hold, while isolating a bug by reverting the one change she made
j.notes: 'The whole encumbrance' and 'sequester that rule somewhere' are misused; 'semi-semicolon' is nonsense. Swapping lat/lon for both points would not usually give 11,000 km (only if one point is swapped), so the bug is under-specified.

j.learned_fact: Coin flips are independent: after four heads in a row the chance of tails on the next flip is still 50 percent (the gambler's fallacy).
j.thinking_skill: distinguishing independent events from perceived streaks, and separating fairness from kindness
j.notes: The laundry/skincare thread and the coin thread are joined only by the narrator asserting they feel like the same insight; 'reifying' in the mother's dialogue feels planted, though it is used correctly.
